profiles.name: Gil Stratton
profiles.excerpt: Gil Stratton moved easily between dramatic radio and sports broadcasting, building a second career behind the microphone after appearing on stage and screen.
profiles.bio_html:
Gil Stratton Jr. was born in Brooklyn in 1922 and entered professional acting while still young. He appeared on Broadway in Best Foot Forward, served in the Army Air Forces during World War II, and settled in Southern California after the war. Radio became a substantial part of his postwar acting career, with appearances on comedy, drama and anthology programs alongside his film work.

Stratton later made broadcasting itself a second profession. Beginning in the 1950s, he became a prominent Southern California sportscaster and sports anchor, working for KNXT television and later KNX radio. He covered events ranging from the Olympics to professional football and horse racing, and his long announcing career makes hosting and narration an important second branch of his public profile rather than an incidental credit.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Stratton, nine This Is Your FBI appearances, eight each on Fibber McGee and Molly and The Line Up, six Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and additional work on The Halls of Ivy, The Great Gildersleeve and The Whistler.

profiles.name: James McCallion
profiles.excerpt: James McCallion began acting as a child and sustained a five-decade career across stage, radio, film and television, with Johnny Dollar forming the largest concentration of his GRH radio work.
profiles.bio_html:
James McCallion was born in Londonderry, Ireland in 1918 and came to the United States as a child. He began acting professionally at seven and made his Broadway debut soon afterward. Radio was part of his career from an early age, including the program Billy and Betty, before stage and film opportunities brought him to Hollywood.

After Army service during World War II, McCallion resumed a career that moved constantly among radio, film and television. His screen credits eventually included Vera Cruz, North by Northwest and PT 109, while television brought him a regular role on National Velvet. Radio remained a continuing professional outlet, particularly in the West Coast dramatic repertory that supplied detective, western and anthology programs.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 44 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to McCallion, nine Broadway Is My Beat appearances, five Theater Five episodes, four Columbia Workshop broadcasts, three The Six Shooter appearances and additional work on CBS Radio Mystery Theater, The Line Up and This Is Your FBI.

profiles.name: Raymond Toyo
profiles.excerpt: Raymond Toyo was the first Kato heard beside the Green Hornet, helping establish one of adventure radio's best-known partnerships during the WXYZ program's formative years.
profiles.bio_html:
Raymond Toyo was the professional name used by Tokutaro Hayashi, an actor in the original Detroit company of The Green Hornet. Director James Jewell gave Hayashi the name Raymond Toyo for broadcasting, and Toyo became the first performer to play Kato, Britt Reid's trusted companion and partner in the Green Hornet's campaign against crime.

Toyo worked during the period when WXYZ was developing The Green Hornet from a local Detroit production into a network property. Kato was essential to the premise from the beginning: he helped maintain Britt Reid's secret identity, drove the Black Beauty and participated directly in the Hornet's operations. Later actors inherited the part, but Toyo's performances helped define the character before the series reached its widest national audience.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 75 The Green Hornet performances credited to Raymond Toyo. Because his surviving GRH work is concentrated entirely in that series, the archive offers a substantial record of his contribution to the program's original ensemble and to the early development of Kato on American radio.

profiles.name: Charles Webster
profiles.excerpt: Charles Webster brought years of stock-company experience into radio, starring as Pat Abbott before becoming a versatile New York dramatic repertory actor.
profiles.bio_html:
Charles Webster, often billed as Chuck Webster, was born and raised in Pittsburgh and spent years working with stock companies before entering radio in his hometown. He later spent six years at a Detroit station, where he had his own program, Know Your America, before moving with his family to New York in 1945.

Webster quickly became a network leading man. He starred opposite Julie Stevens as Pat Abbott in the Mutual comedy-mystery Abbott Mysteries, adapted from Frances Crane's novels, and also appeared on Official Detective. His later credits show the range expected of a New York radio professional, extending from crime programs and supernatural drama to science fiction such as X Minus One.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven The Falcon performances credited to Webster, four Dr. Christian appearances, three X Minus One episodes, two each on Columbia Workshop, Gang Busters, The Clock and The Mysterious Traveler, and additional work on Cloak and Dagger.

profiles.name: Richard Beals
profiles.excerpt: Richard Beals turned a naturally youthful voice into a remarkable radio and voice-acting career, playing children and young characters long before becoming famous as Speedy Alka-Seltzer.
profiles.bio_html:
Richard Beals, known professionally as Dick Beals, was born in Detroit in 1927. A glandular condition kept his voice naturally childlike into adulthood, and while studying at Michigan State he was encouraged to use that unusual vocal quality professionally. Radio became his entry into acting, beginning with Detroit productions including The Lone Ranger and The Green Hornet.

After moving to Hollywood in 1952, Beals became one of the industry's most distinctive voice specialists. He could play boys and girls convincingly without being a child performer, which made him valuable in radio, television and animation. His best-known commercial role was Speedy Alka-Seltzer, and he later voiced characters including Gumby and Davey on Davey and Goliath, while continuing dramatic work on programs such as Dragnet and Gunsmoke.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Gunsmoke performances credited to Beals, seven Suspense appearances, six Wild Bill Hickok episodes, five CBS Radio Workshop broadcasts, four each on Have Gun, Will Travel, The Lone Ranger, The Railroad Hour and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar.

profiles.name: Paul Hecht
profiles.excerpt: Paul Hecht brought classical stage training and a distinguished Broadway career to the repertory of CBS Radio Mystery Theater, where radio remained a major part of his professional life.
profiles.bio_html:
Paul Hecht was born in London in 1941 and trained at the National Theatre School of Canada. He reached Broadway in 1968 with Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, earning a Tony Award nomination for his performance, and went on to a long career in theater, film and television.

Hecht also became one of the most prolific actors in Himan Brown's CBS Radio Mystery Theater. The series demanded performers who could create a complete new character with little more than voice and timing, and Hecht returned repeatedly throughout its run. His later voice work included audiobooks and other spoken-word performance, extending the same microphone craft beyond network drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 72 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Hecht. That concentrated body of work makes his profile a strong example of how formally trained stage actors helped sustain professional radio drama during its major 1970s and 1980s revival.

profiles.name: Tony Randall
profiles.excerpt: Before The Odd Couple made Tony Randall a television star, he was a stage-trained radio actor whose Reggie York became a central voice in the postwar revival of I Love a Mystery.
profiles.bio_html:
Tony Randall was born in Tulsa, Oklahoma in 1920 and trained for the stage at Northwestern University and New York's Neighborhood Playhouse, where he studied with Sanford Meisner. He worked as a radio announcer at WTAG in Worcester, Massachusetts before World War II, then served in the Army Signal Corps and returned to acting after the war.

One of Randall's first major postwar roles was Reggie York in Carlton E. Morse's New York revival of I Love a Mystery, which began in 1949. Opposite Russell Thorson as Jack Packard and Jim Boles as Doc Long, Randall restored the third member of the A-1 Detective Agency to the series after the character had been absent from later years of the original run. The role preceded the Broadway and television work that eventually made Randall nationally famous.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 72 I Love a Mystery performances credited to Randall. That concentrated collection captures an important early chapter of his career and preserves his work in one of radio adventure's most celebrated ensembles before his later success on stage, film and television.

profiles.name: Jim Fletcher
profiles.excerpt: Jim Fletcher learned radio from both sides of the microphone at WXYZ, creating sound effects for The Lone Ranger before becoming one of the program's regular actors.
profiles.bio_html:
Jim Fletcher was part of the close-knit production company at Detroit station WXYZ, where adventure programs such as The Lone Ranger were built live from voices, music and practical sound effects. He first worked behind the scenes as a sound-effects man, handling effects alongside colleagues such as Ernie Winstanley, before moving into acting.

That technical background placed Fletcher inside the physical craft of radio drama before he became one of its performers. Recollections of the WXYZ studios describe sound men producing hoofbeats, chopping, footsteps and other effects in real time while the cast worked only feet away. Fletcher later crossed that studio boundary and became a recurring actor on The Lone Ranger, making sound and technical work a genuine second profession in his GRH taxonomy.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 71 The Lone Ranger performances credited to Fletcher. His surviving GRH record is concentrated in that series, documenting a radio professional who contributed both to the voices listeners heard and to the practical studio craft that made the Ranger's world audible.

profiles.name: John Stephenson
profiles.excerpt: John Stephenson began as a postwar radio actor and announcer before becoming one of American television animation's most prolific voices, including Mr. Slate on The Flintstones.
profiles.bio_html:
John Winfield Stephenson was born in Kenosha, Wisconsin in 1923. During World War II he served as a radio operator and gunner, then studied speech and drama at Northwestern University and worked in Chicago radio. He moved to Hollywood in 1948 and quickly established himself as a working radio actor.

Stephenson's microphone career broadened into announcing, narration, commercials and eventually animation. He introduced episodes of I Love Lucy, narrated the verdict sequences on the later television version of Dragnet, and became a mainstay of Hanna-Barbera voice acting, most famously as Mr. Slate on The Flintstones. His radio credits show the dramatic foundation beneath that later voiceover career.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 18 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Stephenson, 14 The Whistler appearances, seven Wild Bill Hickok episodes, four each on NBC University Theater, Night Beat, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe and This Is Your FBI, plus three Screen Directors Playhouse broadcasts.

profiles.name: Joseph Julian
profiles.excerpt: Joseph Julian was a quintessential New York radio repertory actor, working with Norman Corwin and across thousands of broadcasts before recording the profession from the inside in his memoir This Was Radio.
profiles.bio_html:
Joseph Julian, born Joseph Shapiro in Pennsylvania, entered acting through the stage and made his Broadway debut in 1934. Radio soon became an ideal companion to theater work, and Julian developed into one of New York broadcasting's dependable dramatic actors, appearing in daytime serials, crime programs, anthology drama and experimental productions.

His most important creative partnership was with Norman Corwin. After working on This Is War, Julian became the central American voice in Corwin's acclaimed wartime series An American in England and later returned for other Corwin productions. His career stretched across radio's changing decades, and in 1975 he published This Was Radio, a personal memoir that preserved a working actor's view of the medium and its studio culture.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten X Minus One performances credited to Julian, nine CBS Radio Mystery Theater appearances, eight CBS Radio Workshop broadcasts, six each on Cloak and Dagger and Dimension X, five The Shadow performances and four each on Casey, Crime Photographer and Inner Sanctum Mysteries.
